beats.say: A model is midway through an answer when another person sends a longer prompt. The first request needs one more decoding step. The new request needs its prompt processed. Both compete for the next GPU step and for memory that grows with their histories.

vLLM organizes that serving problem beneath a familiar API. The request front end handles inputs and streaming. An engine schedules token work and manages cached attention state. GPU workers turn that schedule into model execution. Following these boundaries helps explain where a request actually waits.

We will keep the two request identities visible as their histories acquire blocks, share an exact prefix and enter a token budget. Then we will release one request and safely reuse its storage. The useful outcome is a correct response delivered within a latency target.

The offline LLM class accepts prompts through a synchronous Python interface. Synchronous describes what that caller waits for; engine and worker processes can still run separately. Online serving accepts HTTP requests and streams replies. A generation model, a pooling model and a reranker do not automatically implement every route exposed by a familiar API shape.

This source walkthrough pins vLLM zero point twenty-eight point zero, released August twenty-six, twenty twenty-six. The article also checked zero point thirty-one point zero, released October fifth. Our arithmetic programs run on the CPU without importing vLLM, loading model weights or executing a serving engine. The request trace assumes decoder-only full attention, with speculation, offload and hybrid cache groups excluded.

Use vllm serve for the online entrypoint. In zero point thirty, the older Python API-server module became a deprecated compatibility shim, and ordinary scale-out routes require the enable-scale-out flag. A copied environment variable can leave a route absent. Preserve the installed revision, registered routes and resolved configuration before comparing requests or attributing a capability to the engine.

Begin with a constructed memory example. A request reserves twelve token positions but finishes after seven. Five positions remain unused inside its reservation. That is internal fragmentation. Now put two free positions in one region and three in another. Five positions are free overall, yet a request needing four contiguous positions cannot fit into either region. That is external fragmentation.

Fixed-size KV blocks let the request grow by acquiring another physical block without requiring its neighbors. The request keeps its own logical order in a table. Physical placement can change without permuting that logical sequence. A final partly occupied block still has unused cells, so block paging manages fragmentation rather than promising zero waste.

Each cached position holds attention keys and values for the relevant layers and heads. Our four-position blocks make addresses inspectable; actual supported block sizes depend on the backend. For a zero-based position, divide by block size and discard the fraction for its logical block. The remainder gives its within-block offset; the table maps that logical block to a physical ID. Keep the same token identities while changing the view.

Autoregressive decoding reuses keys and values computed for earlier positions. Reserving each request's maximum history would leave unused capacity when it finishes early. vLLM divides cached state into fixed-size blocks and gives each request a table that names its physical blocks.

Our small sentence occupies two four-position blocks. The first lives in one physical slot and the next in another, far away in the pool. Logical order comes from the request's table. The model can read a continuous history without requiring adjacent physical storage.

Follow the selected position through integer division and its within-block offset. A kernel consumes that mapping when loading attention state. Paged addressing describes a memory contract. The actual attention implementation still depends on the model, hardware, dtype and enabled features.

The twenty twenty-three PagedAttention paper reported two to four times higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at comparable latency in its experiments. Its basic sampling workloads used OPT thirteen, sixty-six and one hundred seventy-five billion parameter models with ShareGPT and Alpaca length distributions and Poisson arrivals. Shared-prefix experiments used LLaMA thirteen billion and WMT sixteen translation examples.

Those measurements used GCP A2 instances with A100 GPUs. FasterTransformer had a custom dynamic batcher; the authors reimplemented Orca with different reservation variants. Most traces lasted one hour, while the largest OPT experiment used fifteen minutes. The reported latency was mean end-to-end latency normalized by output length. It does not become a current first-token or tail inter-token guarantee.

The durable mechanism is paged memory and the work it permits. For a new comparison, hold hardware, topology, versions, model, dtypes, sampling, arrivals, lengths, warmup and correctness checks constant. Measure useful completions and latency distributions on that workload. Paged block addressing can feed several current attention kernels; the paper title alone does not identify which kernel a request executed.

In the documented V1 online multiprocessing topology, API servers parse requests, tokenize, load media and stream outputs. They connect through ZeroMQ to engine cores, one per data-parallel rank. Each core owns scheduling and KV management. Each GPU has a worker. With data parallelism, API-server count defaults to the number of ranks, and every API server can reach every engine core.

Let A count API servers, D count data-parallel ranks and N count GPUs. Add A, D and N, then add one coordinator when D exceeds one. Four GPUs with tensor parallelism four and one data-parallel rank give one plus one plus four, or six main processes. Eight GPUs with two-way tensor parallelism and four data-parallel ranks give four plus four plus eight plus one, or seventeen.

This counts the specified serving topology, not every OS process or every offline and Ray deployment. A tokenization stall belongs at the API boundary; queueing and block allocation belong at the core; a collective or kernel belongs at the workers. CPU starvation can delay the GPU handoff even when the GPU has spare capacity. Preserve that ownership while tracing one request ID.

The second sentence begins with the same words and later diverges. In this full-attention teaching path, automatic prefix caching reuses complete matching blocks. Compare the first block, then inspect the next one. A partially matching block does not provide an exact cached block for the new request.

Both requests can point to the first physical slot. Its reference count becomes two. The new request still computes the divergent suffix and its partial final block. The shared-prefix count and skipped-computation count differ because the cache's reuse unit is a whole block.

Cache identity also includes preceding context and relevant configuration, such as an adapter or an enforced trust namespace. Equal text alone cannot establish compatible state. Reuse saves prompt processing. Each new generated token still needs its decoding computation, even when much of the prompt was cached.

The pinned full-attention reference takes the smaller of the shared-prefix length and prompt length minus one. Divide that limit by block size, discard the fractional part, then multiply by block size. The result counts skipped input positions. Subtract skipped positions from prompt length to obtain remaining computation. This assumes eligible cached blocks exist and their complete context matches. For a new request with a block-aligned reused prefix, round the remaining count upward to a whole number of new blocks.

For our nine-position prompt and four-position blocks, six matching positions permit four skips and leave five computations. Seven matching positions give the same result. Eight matching positions permit eight skips and leave one. Turning APC on in the earlier six-position scheduling step would let R0 consume one decode input and R1 compute its remaining five prompt inputs in that same step.

Now make the prompt itself eight positions long, with all eight cached. KV entries do not contain the final logits needed to sample its reply. The pinned code caps the hit at seven positions; block alignment rounds that to four, so the last whole block is recomputed. A one-position prompt skips zero. Sliding-window, hybrid-state, offloaded and prompt-logprob paths require their own contracts.

A block hash includes its parent hash, its exact token IDs and extra context such as adapter identity, multimodal input hashes and an optional cache salt. The parent preserves earlier context: the same suffix after different prefixes can have different attention state. Full-block equality therefore covers more than the visible words in the selected block.

Serialization can fail before the hash function runs. In the pinned zero point twenty-eight implementation, a LoRA named tenant-A with no salt and no LoRA with salt tenant-A both supply the same one-element extra tuple. With the same parent and tokens, the complete hash input is identical. SHA-two-fifty-six cannot distinguish identical serialized input; this is different from two different inputs accidentally sharing a finite digest.

Zero point thirty-one tags extra fields by their source and includes the LoRA path as well as its name. Moving a name to another adapter path can then change cache identity. The documented default uses SHA-two-fifty-six, while non-cryptographic alternatives change the risk tradeoff. Keep the semantic field boundaries, installed version and actual adapter content contract alongside the digest.

The pool preconstructs block objects. A block retains its physical ID, reference count, optional full-block hash and links in a doubly linked free queue. Request tables name their current blocks; a separate hash map finds reusable cached content. A zero reference count can coexist with a cached hash because finished content may still be useful before overwrite.

On a cache hit, touch the matching block. Increase its reference count; if it had zero references, remove it from the free queue first so an allocator cannot overwrite its new reader. New allocations pop queue heads, evict their old hash identities and acquire live references. A hash match and free capacity are consequently related decisions, not interchangeable counters.

For a changed toy queue, suppose the head order is seventy-one, fifty-five, nine, and slot nine is cached. A new request hits nine. Nine leaves that queue and gains a live reference. Another allocation takes seventy-one, leaving only fifty-five free. The request tables, reference counts, free queue and hash map must agree after each operation.

Turn prefix reuse off for this scheduling comparison. The new prompt needs all nine positions computed. With a six-position step budget, admit the active request's decode first. The remaining slots process the first prompt slice. The unprocessed suffix remains attached to the same request identity.

In the next step, decode continues and the remaining prompt positions fit. One budget slot stays unused. Finishing prefill provides the logits for the new request's first sampled output. Budgeted input positions and emitted output tokens describe different parts of the generation loop.

Both requests now decode. The step underfills because their current need is small. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave between steps. A larger prompt slice can reduce the number of prefill steps while lengthening the delay seen by active decodes, so tune against both latency distributions.

To extend the toy scheduler, reserve all ready decode inputs first, subtract them from the step cap, then take the smaller of the remaining budget and prompt work left. Continuous batching changes the active membership between steps. Chunked prefill changes how much of one prompt participates in a step. Those operations can occur together while keeping the request identities fixed.

Use a supplied cost model: each step costs two milliseconds plus one millisecond per computed input position. With our six-position cap, the first mixed step computes six inputs and lasts eight milliseconds. The second computes five and lasts seven. These are constructed durations, not vLLM measurements. Show R0 waiting through those actual extents while R1 retains its unprocessed suffix.

Raise the cap to ten. One R0 input plus all nine prompt inputs now fit in a single twelve-millisecond toy step. R1 finishes prefill in fewer steps, while the active decode waits longer for this first result. Actual GPU costs are nonlinear, so measure first-token and inter-token distributions. Neither the guide’s suggested large caps nor a versioned default supplies a universal optimum.

Zero point thirty-one adds a separate maximum-active-sequences cap for the RUNNING set. With an execution capacity of two hundred fifty-six sequences and an active cap of sixty-four, the sixty-fifth running request still waits even if token slots remain. The token cap, sequence execution capacity and live running-set limit constrain different quantities.

When KV capacity runs out, V1’s default preemption mode is recompute. The engine frees a running request’s blocks, retains the request record and returns it to waiting with computation reset. Its retained tokens can be processed again when capacity returns; cached eligible prefixes may survive elsewhere. Generated tokens do not simply disappear from the user’s request identity.
